# Big picture: Why do we have to make assumptions?

## Why do we have to make assumptions?

<br>

![](figs/gen-process.svg){fig-align="center" height="250"}

<br>

**An example of a model's constraint:**

- Linear models can only model associations between predictors and outcomes as straight lines.
- We cannot change that the model uses straight lines only.
- So if we use linear models, we have to **assume** that a straight line is a reasonable way of representing the actual data generating process in the world.

<br>

**A model's unchangeable constraints = the assumptions that we must be satisfied with in order to use and interpret the model.**



# Assumptions

## What we must assume about the data

```{=html}
<table>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <td><b>Assumption</b></td>
    <td><b>Looks fine</b></td>
    <td><b>Suspicious</b></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle"><b>L</b></td>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle; visibility: hidden;"><b>Linearity:</b> The association between predictor and outcome is close enough to a straight line.</td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/assump-perf.svg" width="350px"/></td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/nonlin.svg" width="350px"/></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle"><b>I</b></td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><b>Independence:</b> Every data point's error is independent of every other data point's error. (Until DAPR3, we'll assume this is true as long as we have between-participant data.)</td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"></td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle"><b>N</b></td>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle; visibility: hidden;"><b>Normally-distributed errors:</b> The differences between fitted line and each data point (i.e., the residuals) are close enough to following a normal distribution.</td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/assump-perf.svg" width="150px"/></td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/nonnorm.svg" width="150px"/></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle;"><b>E</b></td>
    <td style="vertical-align: middle; visibility: hidden;"><b>Equal variance of errors:</b> The differences between fitted line and each data point (i.e., the residuals) are dispersed by a similar enough amount across the whole range of the predictor.</td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/assump-perf.svg" width="150px"/></td>
    <td style="visibility: hidden;"><img src="figs/unequal.svg" width="150px"/></td>
  </tr>
</table>
```

# L is for linear association

## **L**: The association between predictor and outcome is linear

<br>

```{r fig nonlin, message = FALSE, warning=F, echo=F, fig.asp = .5, fig.width = 12}
set.seed(221020)
quadr <- function(x, a, b, c){ a + b*x + c*x^2  }

x <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 101)

df_nonlin <- tibble(
  y = abs(quadr(x + 0.5, 1, 0, 1) + rnorm(101, 0, 1)),
  x1 = abs(1 + (3 * y) + rnorm(101, 0, 1)),
  x2 = x
)
# pairs(df_nonlin)

p_good <- df_nonlin %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=x1, y=y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth=2) +
  labs(
    title = 'Linear (straight line)'
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 28),
  ) +
  NULL

p_quad <- df_nonlin |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x2, y=y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth=2) +
  labs(
    y = element_blank(),
    title = 'Non-linear'
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 28),
  ) +
  NULL

p_good + p_quad
```

## Checking linearity

<br>

If we have only categorical predictors, we don't have to check linearity.
We can just accept that we'll model the difference between group means using a straight line.

<br>

But for continuous predictors (in single/multiple regression models), we check linearity visually using **component–residual plots.**

- **"Component":** The association between one particular predictor and the outcome, with all the other predictors held constant.
  - Think of this as each predictor's individual contribution to the overall linear model.

- **"Residual":** The differences between the line the model predicts and the actual observed data points.

<br>

Basically, component–residual plots can look at the linearity of each association individually, without any of the other predictors getting in the way.



## Component–residual plots

<!-- A component–residual plot shows: -->

<!-- - **x axis:** a predictor across its full range -->
<!-- - **y axis:** that predictor's component + each data point's residual -->

```{r eval=F}
m1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_nonlin)
car::crPlots(m1)
```


```{r fig.asp = .5, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
m1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_nonlin)

car::crPlots(
  m1,
  cex.axis = 2,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex = 2
  )
```

We want the wobbly pink line to match the straight blue line as closely as possible.
Deviations indicate non-linearity.

**We must decide: is the association linear *enough* that it's OK to model the association using a straight line?**

If we aren't willing to make this assumption: try transforming the predictor or outcome variables (e.g., using `log(y)` instead of just plain `y`, or `log(x2)` instead of just plain `x2`).
Then see if the deviation lessens.

<!-- This is a judgement call. There is no single correct answer. -->
<!-- You'll develop a clearer sense of this with time and experience. -->

# I is for independence of errors

## **I**: Independence of errors

<br>

<!-- **If you roll a 20-sided die at 9 am everyday,** you'll generate a lot of values between 1 and 20. -->

<!-- What you roll today is not correlated at all with the number you rolled yesterday. -->

<!-- This was an illustration using autocorrelated **data points**. -->

<!-- Strictly speaking, the linear model assumes that it's the **errors**, not the data points, that are independent—but where data points are autocorrelated, then often the errors are too. -->


The most common source of non-independence is when multiple observations are gathered from the same source.

<br>

For example:

- many test scores gathered from the same schools,
- many reaction times gathered from the same participants,
- and so on.

<br>


:::{.dapr2callout style='font-size: 120%;' .fragment}
**Until DAPR3,** you can assume that errors are independent **as long as the experimental design is between-subjects** (i.e., as long as each person only contributes data to one experimental condition).
:::

# N is for normally-distributed errors

## **N**: Normally-distributed errors

<br>

```{r fig beta, message = FALSE, warning=F, echo=F, fig.asp = .5, fig.width = 12}
# draw errors from a beta distribution, so they're all skewed
set.seed(1)
beta_errors <- rbeta(101, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 50) |> 
  scale(scale = FALSE, center = TRUE) * 50

df_nonnorm <- tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 101),
  y_norm = abs(4 + (2 * x) + rnorm(101, 0, 1)), 
  y_nonnorm = abs(4 + (2 * x) + beta_errors),
)

p_good <- df_nonnorm |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_norm)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(
    y = 'y',
    title = 'Normal errors'
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 32)) +
  NULL

p_beta <- df_nonnorm |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_nonnorm)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(y = 'y') +
  labs(
    y = element_blank(),
    title = 'Non-normal errors'
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 32)) +
  NULL

p_good + p_beta
```


The differences between the fitted line and each data point (aka the **residuals**) should be normally-distributed.

Check normality using **a Q-Q plot.**

```{r include=F}
m_norm <- lm(
  y_norm ~ x, 
  data = df_nonnorm
)

m_nonnorm <- lm(
  y_nonnorm ~ x, 
  data = df_nonnorm
)
```

## Q-Q plots (Quantile–Quantile plots)

Q-Q plots compare the model's residuals (dots) to what the residuals WOULD look like in a world where they were perfectly normally-distributed (diagonal line).
**We want the dots to closely match the diagonal line.**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

**Normally-distributed errors:**

```{r eval=F}
plot(m_norm, which = 2)
```

```{r fig.asp=.7, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 0))  # bltr
plot(
  m_norm, which = 2, 
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```

<!-- A few small divergences at the extremes. -->

:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

**Non-normally-distributed errors:**

```{r eval=F}
plot(m_nonnorm, which = 2)
```

```{r fig.asp=.7, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 0))  # bltr
plot(
  m_nonnorm, which = 2, 
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```

<!-- Bottom left and top right diverge a *lot*! -->

:::
::::

**We must decide: is the distribution of errors normal enough that it's OK to model them using the linear model machinery?**

If we're not willing to make this assumption: 

- Transforming variables is often a good trick.
For example, does the situation improve if you model `log(y)` instead of just `y`?
- Or: bootstrap your model (more next week!).

# E is for equal variance of errors

## **E**: Equal variance of errors


```{r fig unequal, message = FALSE, warning=F, echo=F, fig.asp = .5, fig.width = 12}
set.seed(1)
inc_errors <- rnorm(101, mean = 0, sd = seq(0.1, 4, length.out = 101))

df_unequal <- tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 101),
  y_equal = abs(4 + (2 * x) + rnorm(101, 0, 1)), 
  y_unequal = abs(4 + (2 * x) + inc_errors),
)

p_good <- df_unequal |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_equal)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(
    y = 'y',
    title = 'Errors have\nequal variance'
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 32)) +
  NULL

p_unequal <- df_unequal |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_unequal)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(y = 'y') +
  labs(
    y = element_blank(),
    title = 'Errors have\nunequal variance'
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 32)) +
  NULL

p_good + p_unequal
```

- Equal variance of errors is also called **"homoscedasticity"** or **"homogeneity of errors"**.
- Unequal variance of errors is also called **"heteroscedasticity"** or **"heterogeneity of errors"**.

When errors don't have equal variance, the model is not equally good at estimating the outcome for all values of the predictor.

**Check by plotting the residuals against the fitted (predicted) outcome values.**

```{r include=F}
m_equal <- lm(
  y_equal ~ x, 
  data = df_unequal
)

m_unequal <- lm(
  y_unequal ~ x, 
  data = df_unequal
)
```


## Residuals vs fitted plots

<!-- - **x axis:** the predicted outcome values (aka the "fitted values" across their whole range). -->
<!-- - **y axis:** the residuals of each data point. -->

We want to see a random-looking cloud of data points with the same vertical distance from 0 across the whole x axis.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Errors with equal variance:**

```{r eval=F}
plot(m_equal, which = 1)
```


```{r fig.asp=.6, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 0))  # bltr

plot(
  m_equal, which = 1, 
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Errors with unequal variance:**

```{r eval=F}
plot(m_unequal, which = 1)
```


```{r fig.asp=.6, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 0))  # bltr

plot(
  m_unequal, which = 1, 
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```
:::
::::

**We must decide: is the variance of errors equal enough that it's OK to model the data using the linear model machinery?**

If you are not willing to make this assumption:

- Check if the model is misspecified (e.g., are you missing important covariates or interactions?). Fitting a more suitable model might tidy up the unequal variance.
- Bootstrap the model (more next week!)

## Residuals vs fitted plots also check linearity

Sometimes component-residual plots aren't possible (e.g., in Block 3 when our models contain interactions).

In those cases, we'll check linearity of association using the residuals vs fitted plots.

We want the red line to be straight and flat, closely matching the (tiny) dotted black line at y = 0.

<br>

```{r fig.asp=.6, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
  cex.axis = 1.5,

  cex = 1.5
)
```

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

```{r eval=F}
plot(m_unequal, which = 1)
```


```{r fig.asp=.6, fig.width=7, echo=F, fig.align = 'center'}
par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 0))  # bltr

plot(
  m_unequal, which = 1, 
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```
:::
::::

Same question as always: based on these plots, are we willing to accept that the association is linear enough that a linear model can tell us something useful about our data?

## How can one point influence a model?

<br>

```{r fig infl, message = FALSE, warning=F, echo=F, fig.asp = .5, fig.align='center', fig.width = 12}
set.seed(221020)

n_obs <- 32

df_infl <- tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = n_obs),
  y_good = abs(4 + (2 * x) + rnorm(n_obs, 0, 1)),
  y_infl = y_good,
)

df_infl <- rbind(
  df_infl,
  tibble(
    x = -1.5, y_good = NA, y_infl = 9.5
  )
) |>
  slice_sample(n = n_obs+1)

p_good <- df_infl |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_good)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(
    y = 'y',
    title = "If it's removed, the line\nmoves down!"
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 24)) +
  NULL

p_infl <- df_infl |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y_infl)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(y = 'y') +
  labs(
    y = element_blank(),
    title = 'A dataset with one\ninfluential observation'
    ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 24)) +
  NULL

p_infl + p_good
```


To see how much each data point influences the model's estimates, we use a measure called **Cook's distance.**


## Cook's distance

<br>

Cook's distance measures **the average distance that the predicted outcome values will move, if a given data point is removed** (mathy details in back matter).


```{r include=F}
m_infl <- lm(y_infl ~ x, df_infl)
m_good <- lm(y_good ~ x, df_infl)
```

<br>

Find each data point's Cook's distance using `cooks.distance()`:

```{r}
cooks.distance(m_infl) |> head()
```

<br>

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="30%"}

Or, more usefully, make a plot:

```{r eval=F}
plot(
  m_infl,
  which = 4
)
```
:::
:::{.column width="70%"}

```{r echo=F, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.align = 'center'}
plot(
  m_infl,
  which = 4,
  cex.axis = 1.5,
  cex.lab = 1.5,
  cex.caption = 1.5,
  cex.id = 1.5,
  cex = 1.5
)
```
:::
::::


Data point 25 has by far the greatest influence on the model's estimates.

# Sensitivity analysis

## Sensitivity analysis

<br>

A sensitivity analysis asks: **Do our conclusions change if we leave out the unusual data point?**

Specific coefficient values will almost definitely change, but **our actual conclusions are usually based on (a) the direction of the slope estimate and (b) whether or not we reject its H0 at our chosen $\alpha$ level, usually .05.**

- If our conclusions don't change, then the influential data point doesn't actually matter, regardless of how big its Cook's distance is.
- If our conclusions DO change, then we need to 
  - report this as a limitation of our analysis and
  - draw our conclusions based on the newer model.

<br>

We saw that the influential data point is in row 25, so we will remove that one row from the data and re-fit the model.

```{r}
m_infl_sens <- lm(
  y_infl ~ x, 
  data = df_infl[-25,]  # "subtract" row 25 (notation: [rownum, colnum])
)
```


## Compare coefficient estimates

<br>

From the original model, fit to the data that **contains** the high-influence value: 

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  summary(m_infl)
), '\n')[9:12])
```

<br>

From the new model, fit to the data with the high-influence value **removed**:


```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  summary(m_infl_sens)
), '\n')[9:12])
```


<br>

The values of the coefficients do change a bit, but the association is still positive, and it's still significant.

**$\rightarrow$ Even though the high-influence point had a big Cook's Distance, it doesn't affect our conclusions.**

So we could just write something like 

> One observation had a much higher Cook's distance than all the others, but a sensitivity analysis showed that this observation does not affect the direction of associations or the pattern of significance of our results.



# Multicollinearity

## Multicollinearity

::: {.r-stack}
![](figs/collinear1.svg){.fragment height="600" }

![](figs/collinear2.svg){.fragment height="600" }

![](figs/collinear3.svg){.fragment height="600" }

![](figs/collinear4.svg){.fragment height="600" }

:::

:::{.fragment}

When two predictors are correlated, they contain similar information.

**If you know one, you can guess the other.**

The model cannot tell which predictor is contributing what information, so its estimates are less precise.

Technically speaking, **the variance of its estimates increases,** and a significant result is less likely.

:::


<!-- ## Correlated predictors -->

```{r include=F}
set.seed(1)

n_obs <- 101
corr_x1y  <- 0.8
corr_x2y  <- 0.6
# corr_x1x2 <- 0.9  # vif = 5.3
corr_x1x2 <- 0.93   # vif = TBD

corr_df <- MASS::mvrnorm(
  n = n_obs,
  mu = c(0, 0, 0),
  Sigma = matrix(
    c(1, corr_x1y, corr_x2y,
     corr_x1y, 1, corr_x1x2,
     corr_x2y, corr_x1x2, 1),
    nrow = 3),
  empirical = TRUE
  )

colnames(corr_df) <- c('y', 'x1', 'x2')
corr_df <- as_tibble(corr_df)
```



## Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)

<br>

We measure how much the variance has been inflated by correlated predictors using the **Variance Inflation Factor** or VIF.

VIF measures **how much the standard error of a predictor is increased by correlations with other predictors** (mathy details in the back matter).

<br> 

Intepreting VIF:

- **Close to 1 is ideal.**
- **Below 5 is low,** no need to worry.
- **Between 5 and 10 is moderate,** start to worry here.
- **More than 10 is severe,** very not good.

If VIF > 5, remove one of the correlated predictors (it's not adding anything new anyway), or combine them into a composite score (more on this in DAPR3!)



## VIF in R


Here's a dataset that I simulated to have highly correlated predictors `x1` and `x2`:

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r}
corr_df |> head(8)
```

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
#| code-fold: true

corr_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x1, y =  x2)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```
:::
::::

We calculate the Variance Inflation Factor in R using `vif()` from the package `car`.

Fit a model and compute its VIF:

```{r}
m_corr <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = corr_df)
car::vif(m_corr)
```

VIF > 5, which means that **the variance in the model is much bigger with both predictors included than it would be if either one of them were left out.**

# Back matter {.appendix}

## Revisiting this week's learning objectives

::: {.dapr2callout}
**What must we assume is true about our data, in order to use a linear model?**

- Linearity: The association between predictor and outcome is close enough to a straight line.
- Independence: Every data point is independent of every other data point.
- Normally-distributed errors: The differences between fitted line and each data point (i.e., the residuals) are close enough to following a normal distribution.
- Equal variance of errors: The differences between fitted line and each data point (i.e., the residuals) are dispersed by a similar enough amount across the whole range of the predictor.
:::



::: {.dapr2callout}
**What property of a single data point might affect a linear model's estimates? 
How can we diagnose it?**

- High influence: an unusual value for the outcome and/or the predictor. 
- Diagnose using Cook's Distance.
:::

::: {.dapr2callout}
**What relationship between predictors do we want to avoid? How can we diagnose it?**

- We want to avoid predictors being highly correlated with one another. If they are, we call the situation "multicollinearity".
- When predictors are highly correlated, they contain very similar information, so the model is very uncertain how each one individually is associated with the outcome.
- Diagnose multicollinearity with the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF).
:::

## Cook's Distance: Intuition

<br>

Cook's distance is essentially **outlyingness $\times$ leverage**.

<br>

```{=html}
<table>
  <tr>
    <td>small outlyingness</td>
    <td>x</td>
    <td>small leverage</td>
    <td>=</td>
    <td>small influence</td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>small outlyingness</td>
    <td>x</td>
    <td><b>BIG</b> leverage</td>
    <td>=</td>
    <td><b>BIG</b> influence</td>
  </tr>
    
  <tr>
    <td><b>BIG</b> outlyingness</td>
    <td>x</td>
    <td>small leverage</td>
    <td>=</td>
    <td><b>BIG</b> influence</td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
    <td><b>BIG</b> outlyingness</td>
    <td>x</td>
    <td><b>BIG</b> leverage</td>
    <td>=</td>
    <td><b>VERY BIG</b> influence</td>
  </tr>
</table>
```



## Cook's Distance: Mathy details

<br>

**Cook's Distance** of a data point $i$:


$$D_i = \frac{(\text{StandardizedResidual}_i)^2}{k+1} \times \frac{h_i}{1-h_i}$$

Where

$$\frac{(\text{StandardizedResidual}_i)^2}{k+1} = \text{Outlyingness}$$

and

$$\frac{h_i}{1-h_i} = \text{Leverage},$$

So 

$$D_i = \text{Outlyingness} \times \text{Leverage}.$$



## VIF: Mathy details

<br>

$\sqrt{\text{VIF}}$ = how many times larger the standard error (SE) of each predictor is, compared to a version of the model without the other predictors.

<br> 

The thresholds of 5 and 10:

  - $\sqrt{5} = 2.24$, so SE is 2.24 times bigger than it would be if we removed the correlated predictors.
  - $\sqrt{10} = 3.16$, so SE is 3.16 times bigger than it would be if we removed the correlated predictors.

<br>

For a given predictor $x_j$, VIF is calculated as:  

$$
VIF_j = \frac{1}{1-R_j^2} \\
$$
